---
title: "Native conditional placement and scheduling"
---

`Cellerator::conditional` provides a C++17 host planner and event-driven execution
queue for already selected conditional work. The public headers are
`Cellerator/execution/conditional/topology.hh` and `scheduler.hh`. They reuse the
existing `ExpertKey`, `Origin`, `Selection`, `DispatchPlan`, and `ParameterStore`;
there is no second routing or parameter identity system.

## Logical demand and physical placement

`PlacementPlanner::plan` takes a `DispatchPlan`, an explicit mapping from logical
origins to device IDs, input/output bytes per occurrence, and a caller-defined
work revision. Every duplicate, signed or zero-weight selection survives with
its original occurrence index. Demands group exact expert revision and origin
device; the original `DispatchPlan` retains cell, rank and row provenance and the
weighted inverse combine. Placement does not select different experts when a
revision is unavailable.

`HardwareTopology` consumes device budgets and directed links with bandwidth and
latency. It chooses a deterministic shortest transfer route for the actual
message size, charging every store-and-forward hop. Missing links remain
unreachable; zero-byte transfers have zero cost. Topology is supplied metadata,
not hardware discovery or a claim about measured bandwidth or contention.

`ResidencySnapshot` names immutable expert revisions and records resident and
pending copies, their bytes, execution eligibility, pins and readiness events.
All copies, including pinned old revisions and in-flight reservations, consume
capacity. `other_usage` adds all remaining allocations, such as state,
activation staging, master parameters and optimizer storage. Do not count copy
bytes in both places. A zero device budget means zero capacity. Planning does not
evict copies, so no pinned or pending allocation can be reclaimed implicitly.

For each selected demand the planner compares:

- Local execution against an exact ready or explicitly pending copy.
- Remote activation transfer, execution and return of outputs.
- Temporary weight transfer to the origin, released after that decision.
- A retained replica at the origin, usable by later demands through an explicit
  producer-decision dependency.

Candidate enumeration and exact-cost ties are deterministic. Optional repeat
hints amortize transfer cost when choosing a retained replica; they do not alter
logical selection. Proposed replicas remain proposals and cannot be reported as
actual ready residency. Existing pending sources attach their caller-supplied
completion events to candidates. A failed plan reports the rejected candidates
and the exact demand; it never falls back to another revision.

## Costs and memory boundary

The optional cost callback supplies compute, preparation, allocation and
synchronization seconds for a whole demand on a candidate device. Without it,
compute uses `ExpertSpec::compute_seconds_per_use` and device compute scale; the
other components are explicitly zero. Link estimates add parameter movement,
activation movement and output return. Retention penalty is separately supplied
in seconds per retained byte. These are estimates for a sequential horizon, not
a measured distributed makespan or an overlap model. Repeat hints describe a
forecast horizon; estimates with overlapping hints should not be interpreted as
unique observed work.

The planner accounts for parameter copies, execution input/output workspace,
and return-output storage at the origin. Retained replicas affect subsequent
decisions. `projected_memory` excludes temporary workspace;
`peak_memory` records component-wise high-water marks, which need not coincide;
`peak_total_bytes` records the actual maximum total in this sequential model.
Caller allocations and any intermediate-hop transport staging must be included
in `other_usage`. The backend still admits real allocations and residency pins
against current resources before launching work. A snapshot is not a resource
reservation, and the planner does not implement a mutable residency manager.

## Event-driven native execution

`PlannedExecution` binds a plan to the exact work revision and residency snapshot
generation. It validates occurrence identities/order and replica dependencies,
checks parameter byte sizes, and acquires `ParameterStore` leases for all exact
selected revisions. Publishing and retiring a newer revision cannot substitute
the queued parameters. The caller must supply current generation values and
serialize changes between snapshot admission and backend resource reservation.

The queue has a caller-chosen maximum decision count. `advance(callback, budget)`
runs at most `budget` callbacks and schedules decisions sequentially, matching
the memory model. Each task reports ready, running, yielded, completed or failed.
An unsignaled source-readiness event prevents any callback. A callback returns
`TaskPoll::yield(event)` after starting asynchronous work, then resumes the same
decision after `signal(event)`. The callback must retain its own phase/state and
must not replay transfers or kernels on resume. Signal only events that actually
completed; event identities must not be reused for unrelated in-flight work.

Callbacks receive the original worklist, the decision and an exact immutable
parameter lease. They own physical residency pins, allocations, transfers,
streams, numerical work and output placement. A successful completion means
all device reads/writes are finished and any promised replica is usable.
CUDA/Cytoplast backends can use the same host queue with their own event polling
and device launch adapters. No transport, CUDA copy, CUDA kernel, device event
poller, thread pool or collective implementation is supplied by this queue.

Leases remain until `close()` after completion. On failure, the queue stops
without replay and preserves the completed prefix; the caller drains already
submitted device/transport work before `close(true)`. Keep the queue alive while
asynchronous work or backward still reads its leases. The queue is single-owner
and not thread-safe; synchronize external event delivery. Its destructor is
ordinary C++ lifetime release, not a device synchronization operation.

The runnable [host example](../examples/framework/native/scheduler_example.cc)
uses synthetic completion events and CPU callbacks, then combines results in
original selection order. It demonstrates lifecycle and identity preservation,
not hardware execution or speedup. The focused
[native test](../tests/framework/native/scheduler_test.cc) covers directed
message-size routing, exact revisions, replica dependencies, complete cost
callbacks, pinned/in-flight capacity, stale snapshots, queue bounds and failure
drain. Build target registration is in `cmake/CelleratorConditional.cmake`.
